**Neither, to start with. Build one agent.** More agents don't always give better results, and sometimes they make results worse.

Take a student who asks, "Is the laser cutter free Friday at 3? If so, book it." Booking depends on what the calendar check finds. If you give those jobs to separate agents, one has to hand the details to the other, and "Friday at 3" can arrive as just "Friday". One agent with a few tools avoids that handoff.

The general idea: a **multi-agent system** splits work among several agents that must pass information between them. That can help when a job breaks into independent parts. In a [Google Research study](https://research.google/blog/towards-a-science-of-scaling-agent-systems-when-and-why-agent-systems-work/), multi-agent setups did much better on a parallel finance task, but 39–70% worse on a planning task where each step depended on earlier ones.

Cost matters too. A **token** is a small chunk of text a model reads or writes, and you typically pay per token. [Anthropic reported](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) that in its data, agents used about 4× the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15×. Your numbers will differ, but that's a real risk to a small budget.

For your design review: "We start with one agent, test it on real student questions, and split only if we find a failure that splitting fixes." Good reasons might include independent work that can run side by side, or more material than fits in one **context window** (the most a model can take in at once).

**Your turn:** which is the better candidate for several agents, and why?

- A: checking that a machine is free, then booking it
- B: searching ten separate manuals for their safety warnings

I can turn this into a short lesson if you like.
